1.goal: To open the lesson on what it is about: the same argument said two ways, and only one of them the room can follow.
1.interaction: T–S, one open question. Portuguese is accepted here.
run: Ask about the last presentation where she felt the room lost the thread — in Portuguese or in English.
One answer, and move on.
1.expected: One concrete presentation, most likely one of her own.
1.support: If nothing comes, ask about a talk she sat through as audience and stopped following.
1.challenge: Ask what she did when she noticed the room had lost her, and whether it worked.
1.monitoring: She is a recognized presenter in Portuguese. Do not treat that as a skill to build; treat it as a skill to carry across.
1.evidence: The presentation she names — it is the situation the lesson keeps pointing back to.
1.transition: Move on when she has given one concrete example.

2.goal: To establish who asked, what they asked for, and what she leaves the conversation with.
2.interaction: T–S, reading the message on screen together.
run: Give her time to read.
Confirm two things out loud: the room has NOT read the document, and it is three minutes — not ten.
2.expected: Recognition — and her real situation, with the clock in sight.
2.support: If the brief reads as background, ask what the board will have decided by the end of the meeting.
2.challenge: Ask what she would drop first if it were ninety seconds instead of three minutes.
2.monitoring: Do not anticipate which of the two versions is the good one. The comparison is the work of stage 4.
2.evidence: Whether she can state what the room needs from her in one sentence.
2.transition: Move on when she says, in one sentence, what the room needs from her.

3.goal: To activate what she already knows about why a room loses the thread, BEFORE she sees the texts.
3.interaction: T–S, three open questions. Portuguese accepted, and given back in English.
run: Read the three questions WITH her, out loud, and ask for a guess on each.
Do not correct: these are hypotheses.
If she answers in Portuguese, take the idea and say it back in English for her to repeat. Do not stop the idea to fix the language.
exact: Giving the idea back in English: “So the speaker never said where the argument was going. In English: they did not signpost it. Try that back.”
3.expected: She has repertoire to spare here — forty-one years of presenting. Let her talk; this is one of the few moments in the lesson where a long turn costs nothing.
3.support: If a guess comes in one word, ask “why that one?” once. The reason is what transfers to the production.
3.challenge: Ask which of the three she would defend in front of a room that disagreed.
3.monitoring: Whether the English comes back when you offer it, or whether the idea stays in Portuguese.
3.evidence: The reasons she gives — they are the argument she will use in stage 8.
3.transition: Move on when she has risked all three.

4.goal: To read each version for what it is, before the comparison.
4.interaction: S reads alone in silence, then T–S on one question.
run: Two minutes per version, in silence.
Then ask, without pointing at anything: in which of them did you know, before the end, that a request was coming?
exact: Do both say accuracy is 94%? (Yes.) Do both ask to hold the launch? (Yes.) So what changed? (Only the map.)
4.expected: The facts are the same in both; what changes is whether the room can see where the argument is going.
4.support: If the difference will not come, read the first two sentences of each version out loud, one after the other.
4.challenge: Ask her to name the exact sentence in version B where she first knew a request was coming.
4.monitoring: She will want to judge the business decision — that is her instinct. Hold it: today the object is the FORM of the argument, not its merit.
4.evidence: Whether she separates form from merit on her own. It is the discipline the whole lesson needs.
4.transition: Move on when she says the facts are the same.

5.goal: To separate what CHANGED between the two versions from what was never in either.
5.interaction: S works alone on the six, then T–S on the two limit cases.
run: Let her do it alone and only then open the explanation.
If she gets stuck, send her back to the text to point at the line — do not give the answer.
exact: “Which regulator” — which of the two says it? (Neither.)
5.expected: Two of the six are not supported by one version alone; finding those is the point of the stage.
5.support: If she answers from memory, close the answer and ask her to find the line first.
5.challenge: Ask what she would have to add to the memo for the “neither” item to become supported.
5.monitoring: The “neither of them” item is the one that decides the lesson. It is the question the room would ask, and neither version answers it — which is why she closes it herself at stage 8.
5.evidence: Whether she goes back to the text or answers from memory. It is the first isolated reading measure.
5.transition: Move on when she gets the two limit cases right, with or without a first attempt.

6.goal: To name the difference between SIGNAL, fact and opinion — and to notice that the signal carries no content.
6.interaction: S classifies alone, then T–S on the two questions.
run: She classifies, then open the explanation.
Then ask: which of these could you remove without losing any information? (The signals.) And what is lost then? (The map.)
exact: Does “What this means is…” state any new fact? (No.) So why is it there? (To say that what follows is a consequence, not one more piece of data.)
6.expected: The signals carry the map; the facts and the opinion carry the content.
6.support: If a line resists classification, ask whether the room would learn anything new from it.
6.challenge: Ask her to write one more signal of her own for the same argument.
6.monitoring: She is an executive and will want to argue whether “costs us the license” is fact or opinion. It is opinion, and the discussion is a good one — but two minutes, not five.
6.evidence: Whether she names the signal as the category that adds no content. That naming is what stage 7 practices.
6.transition: Move on when she names the signal as the category that adds no content.

7.goal: To produce the signal out loud, with support on screen, before producing it without.
7.interaction: T gives the bare fact; S gives it back with the move in front. Six, at speed.
run: You say the bare content (“accuracy is 94%”) and she gives back the whole sentence with the signal in front of it. Six of them, fast.
Seven minutes, and the next stage is the longest of the lesson. If she starts discussing the case, cut in gently.
Pronunciation: in “having said THAT” the weight falls on THAT. In “What this MEANS is”, the peak is on MEANS, and the “is” is weak.
exact: If she starts on the case: “That is the three minutes — hold it.”
7.expected: Six sentences, each with the signal before the content, at speed.
7.support: If the signal will not come, give the first three words and let her finish the sentence.
7.challenge: Give two facts at once and ask for one sentence that signals both.
7.monitoring: Whether she still needs the screen by the fifth and sixth.
7.evidence: On how many of the six the signal arrives without support. It is the number to compare with the three minutes.
7.transition: Move on when she places the signal without consulting the screen on the last two.

8.goal: The product of the lesson — three minutes, with the texts out of sight.
8.interaction: Role-play. You are the review board; the turn is hers.
run: CLOSE both texts on the screen before she starts.
Interrupt ONCE, in the middle, with a question of substance, and let her find her way back on her own.
After you ask, WAIT. The turn is hers, and her silence is work.
Do not correct during. Note it and hand it back at stage 9.
If she wants to use her own case instead of the one on screen, accept it — pre-class activity 6 already asked for that, and her own argument is worth more than the invented one.
8.expected: Three minutes that open on where they are, name the problem, and close on the request — with the signals audible.
8.support: If she stalls after the interruption, repeat her last sentence back as a question and wait.
8.challenge: Ask a second question at the end — “and if we ship anyway?” — and take the answer inside the same three minutes.
8.monitoring: Whether the signals survive when the text is off screen, and whether she closes on the request or runs out of time first.
8.evidence: One sentence as she said it, word for word. It is the third field of the next screen.
8.transition: Move on when she closes with the request, or at three minutes, whichever comes first.

9.goal: To hand back what you noted and to ask for it again, in half the time.
9.interaction: T–S, filling the board together, then one retask.
run: Two things at most — one that worked and one where the signal did not come out.
Then the retask: same argument, ninety seconds, and this board already disagrees with her.
Do not add new content here. The retask is the same task under one changed constraint.
exact: Same argument, ninety seconds — and this board already disagrees with you.
9.expected: The same argument with the background gone and the signals kept.
9.support: If she cannot cut, ask what the board already knows now that it has read the memo.
9.challenge: Ask for the same argument in thirty seconds and see what survives twice.
9.monitoring: What she CUTS when the time halves. If the signals go, they are not automatic yet.
9.evidence: What she cut. It goes in the post-lesson record, and it is what lesson 6 decides on.
9.transition: Move on when the ninety seconds have been given.

10.goal: To register what was worked on and to leave the next lesson announced.
10.interaction: S ticks the list and answers the scale; T–S on the close.
run: She ticks what she recognizes. Do not argue with the marks — they are hers.
Homework, said out loud and never on screen: the post-class has one optional recording about a real decision of hers and two TED talks where the signposting is doing visible work.
Announce lesson 4: listening — the Q&A AFTER the presentation, with one clear question, one vague and one hostile, answered on the spot. She will recognize the scene.
exact: The Cathy O'Neil talk is this lesson, done live: she argues about algorithms to people who do not work with them, and she signposts every turn.
10.expected: Some lines ticked, and one honest answer on the confidence row.
10.support: If nothing is ticked, read the list with her and ask which line she would use in her next board meeting.
10.challenge: Ask when the next three-minute slot in her diary is, and which signal she takes into it.
10.monitoring: A low mark on the signals after three minutes that held them is worth recording: it is the gap between doing and knowing that she did.
10.evidence: Fill the post-lesson record BEFORE you close. This is lesson 3 of the 6 in the block; lesson 6 reads the four together and steers the planning that follows.
